# How to use this guide

Pharmaceutical Engineering is the most "machine-heavy" subject of semester 3. Almost every long question asks you to describe one or two pieces of equipment, and almost every short question is either a machine, a law or a definition. Study one unit a day: read the notes, draw every sketch once from memory, then answer the question bank without looking.

**PCI end-semester paper as used by HPTU (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective questions (MCQs, fill in the blanks or one-line answers) | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays: attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers: attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Where marks usually come from**

| Unit | Typical weight | Favourite questions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Heavy | Reynolds number, Bernoulli, venturi/orifice/rotameter, laws of size reduction, ball mill (critical speed), hammer mill, fluid energy mill, cyclone, official powder grades |
| 2 | Heavy | Fourier's law, heat exchangers, climbing film and multiple effect evaporators, economy, steam and molecular distillation, fractional distillation |
| 3 | Heavy | Rate of drying curve, EMC, spray dryer, FBD, freeze dryer, mechanisms of mixing, double cone, ribbon, sigma blade, Silverson |
| 4 | Medium–heavy | Theories and factors of filtration, filter aids, plate and frame, rotary drum, membrane filters, super centrifuge, perforated basket |
| 5 | Medium | Factors for material selection, stainless steel, theories and types of corrosion, prevention, material handling |

**Probability ratings**

- **High:** asked in most years in some form; prepare the full answer with a labelled sketch.
- **Medium:** asked every few years, or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low:** rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice in Section C.

The ratings are estimates from the syllabus weight and the usual pattern of PCI pharmacy papers. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Use the six standard headings for every machine:** Principle → Construction (with a labelled diagram) → Working → Uses → Merits → Demerits. Examiners mark each heading.
2. **Draw the sketch first.** A neat labelled block or line drawing takes two minutes and earns a large share of the marks. Label inlet, outlet, heating medium and moving parts.
3. **Write the equation with every symbol explained:** Re = Duρ/µ, Fourier's law, Darcy's equation, F = mω²r, the three laws of size reduction, economy of evaporation.
4. **Give numbers you are sure of:** laminar Re below about 2000, ball mill optimum at about 0.5–0.75 of critical speed, 0.22 µm membrane for sterilisation, 18/8 stainless steel.
5. **Compare in a table** when a question says "differentiate" (evaporation vs drying, solid vs liquid mixing, orifice vs venturi, perforated vs non-perforated basket).
6. **End with pharmaceutical uses:** name real products (granules, antibiotics, vaccines, syrups, volatile oils). This links engineering to pharmacy and fetches the last marks.
7. **For curves** (rate of drying, sorption isotherm) label both axes and every stage.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only an hour, learn these with full sketches: **ball mill (critical speed)**, **multiple effect evaporator and economy**, **rate of drying curve + spray dryer/FBD/freeze dryer**, **plate and frame filter press + rotary drum filter**, and **theories and prevention of corrosion**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Equations to write without thinking**

| Fanning friction | hf = 4fLu²/2gD; laminar f = 16/Re | 1 |
| Rittinger / Kick / Bond | E = KR(1/L2 − 1/L1); E = KK ln(L1/L2); E = KB(1/√L2 − 1/√L1) | 1 |
| Ball mill critical speed | Nc = (1/2π)√(g/(R − r)) ≈ 42.3/√(D − d) rpm | 1 |
| Stokes' law | v = d²(ρs − ρf)g/18η | 1, 4 |
| Fourier's law | dQ/dt = −kA dT/dx | 2 |

| Filter leaf | Vacuum through a covered screen | Small-scale filtration |
| Rotary drum filter | Continuous vacuum, 5 zones | Fermentation broths, precipitates |
| Meta filter | Stacked metal rings + kieselguhr | Clarifying syrups, oils, injections |
| Membrane / cartridge | Sieving through uniform pores (0.22 µm) | Sterile filtration |
| Seitz filter | Asbestos pad (depth) | Old sterile filtration; fibre shedding |
| Perforated basket | Centrifugal filtration | Crystals from mother liquor |
| Non-perforated basket | Centrifugal sedimentation | Fine solids that clog cloth |
| Super centrifuge | Tubular bowl, very high speed | Immiscible liquids, emulsions |

**Definitions that earn 2 marks**

- **Unit operation:** a basic physical step common to many processes (size reduction, drying, filtration).
- **EMC:** moisture content of a solid in equilibrium with air of given humidity and temperature.
- **Critical moisture content:** moisture at which the constant rate period ends.
- **Filter aid:** inert porous powder that keeps the cake porous (kieselguhr, perlite).
- **Corrosion:** destruction of a metal by chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment.
- **Passivation:** strengthening the oxide film of stainless steel with nitric (or citric) acid.

**Numbers worth memorising**

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Ball mill fill / optimum speed | 30–50% balls; about 0.5–0.75 of critical |
| Fine / very fine powder (IP) | All through sieve 85 / sieve 120 |
| Sieve 85 / 120 aperture | 180 µm / 125 µm |
| Stefan–Boltzmann constant | 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴ |
| Triple point of water | about 0.01 °C, 4.6 mm Hg |
| Sterilising membrane | 0.22 µm (or 0.2 µm) |
| Kozeny constant | about 5 |
| Stainless steel 304 | 18% Cr, 8% Ni; 316 adds Mo |

**Corrosion in five lines**

1. Electrochemical cells form on the metal: anode dissolves (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻).
2. Cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻, or 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H2 in acid.
3. Types: uniform, galvanic, pitting, crevice, intergranular, stress cracking, erosion, dezincification.
4. Prevent by material choice, design, coatings, cathodic protection, inhibitors, environment control, passivation.
5. In a galvanic couple the more active metal (zinc, magnesium) corrodes and protects steel.

# Radiation constant of brass, iron, unpainted and painted glass

**Aim:** To determine the radiation constant (rate of heat loss by radiation) of brass, iron, unpainted glass and painted (black) glass, and to compare them.

> Quantities and set-ups vary between colleges. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Handle hot water and hot vessels with tongs and heat-resistant gloves.

## Principle

Every body above absolute zero emits radiant energy. By the **Stefan–Boltzmann law**, the rate of emission is Q/t = ε σ A T⁴, where ε is the emissivity of the surface. Dark, rough surfaces have high emissivity; polished metals have low emissivity.

In the simple laboratory method, equal containers (or tubes) made of different materials are filled with the same volume of hot water and allowed to cool in still air. The fall in temperature with time is recorded. The heat lost per unit time per unit area per degree of excess temperature gives a comparative **radiation (cooling) constant** of each surface. Surfaces that radiate well cool faster.

By Newton's law of cooling, for small temperature differences: −dT/dt = K (T − Ts), where Ts is the surroundings temperature and K the cooling constant, which depends on the surface.

## Requirements

Containers of the same size and shape made of brass, iron and glass; one glass container painted dull black outside; thermometers (0–110 °C); stopwatch; hot water (about 80–90 °C); measuring cylinder; insulated stands or corks; vernier calipers or scale.

## Procedure

1. Measure the outer diameter and height of each container and calculate its outer surface area (A).
2. Note the room temperature (Ts).
3. Fill each container with the same volume of hot water at the same starting temperature (about 80 °C). Close with a cork carrying a thermometer.
4. Place all containers on insulating stands, away from draughts, at the same distance from one another.
5. Start the stopwatch and record the temperature of each every minute (or every 2 minutes) for 20–30 minutes.
6. Weigh or note the mass of water (m) in each and the mass and specific heat of each container.

## Observations and calculations

| Time (min) | Brass (°C) | Iron (°C) | Unpainted glass (°C) | Painted glass (°C) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 80 | 80 | 80 | 80 |
| 2 | | | | |
| 4 | | | | |
| … | | | | |

1. Plot temperature against time for each surface (cooling curves).
2. From the slope (dT/dt) at a chosen temperature, find the rate of heat loss:
   Q/t = (m × c water + mass of vessel × c vessel) × dT/dt
3. Radiation (cooling) constant = (Q/t) ÷ [A × (T − Ts)]   in W/m²·K
4. Alternatively, plot ln (T − Ts) against time; the slope gives the cooling constant K.

**Worked example (illustration only):** water 200 g (c = 4.18 J/g·K), negligible vessel heat capacity, dT/dt = 0.8 K/min = 0.0133 K/s, A = 0.03 m², T − Ts = 50 K.
Q/t = 200 × 4.18 × 0.0133 ≈ 11.1 W. Constant = 11.1 ÷ (0.03 × 50) ≈ 7.4 W/m²·K.

## Result

The radiation constants of the surfaces were: brass ___, iron ___, unpainted glass ___, painted glass ___ W/m²·K. The painted (black) glass lost heat fastest and polished brass slowest.

## Precautions

1. Use identical containers and the same volume and starting temperature of water.
2. Avoid draughts and keep containers apart so they do not heat one another.
3. Read thermometers at eye level and at exact times.
4. Stir gently before each reading for a uniform temperature.

## Viva questions

1. **State the Stefan–Boltzmann law.** Energy radiated per unit time is proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature: Q/t = εσAT⁴.
2. **What is a black body?** A body that absorbs all radiation falling on it and is the perfect emitter (ε = 1).
3. **What is emissivity?** The ratio of energy radiated by a surface to that by a black body at the same temperature.
4. **Why does painted glass cool faster?** A dull black surface has a higher emissivity, so it radiates more heat.
5. **State Kirchhoff's law.** At the same temperature, emissivity of a body equals its absorptivity.
6. **Why are steam pipes lagged and shiny?** Lagging reduces conduction and convection; shiny surfaces have low emissivity and lose less heat by radiation.

# Efficiency of steam distillation

**Aim:** To carry out steam distillation of a water-immiscible liquid (for example turpentine oil or a volatile oil) and to calculate the efficiency of the process.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Steam and hot glassware cause burns; keep a safety tube in the steam generator.

## Principle

When two immiscible liquids are heated together, each exerts its own full vapour pressure. The mixture boils when the **sum of the two vapour pressures equals atmospheric pressure**, so it boils below 100 °C and below the boiling point of the oil.

The theoretical ratio of the two liquids in the distillate is:

mo / mw = (po × Mo) / (pw × Mw)

where m is mass, p vapour pressure at the boiling temperature and M molecular weight (o = oil, w = water).

In practice the steam does not become fully saturated with oil vapour, so less oil distils than theory predicts. The **efficiency** is:

Efficiency (%) = (actual mass of oil per gram of water ÷ theoretical mass of oil per gram of water) × 100

## Requirements

Steam generator with safety tube, round-bottom distillation flask, Liebig condenser, receiver (measuring cylinder or separating funnel), thermometer, heating mantle or burner, turpentine oil (or clove oil), water, barometer reading, table of vapour pressure of water.

## Procedure

1. Put a known volume of oil (e.g. 20 ml) with a little water in the distillation flask and fit the steam inlet tube to reach near the bottom.
2. Connect the flask to the condenser and receiver. Warm the flask gently so that steam does not condense too much in it.
3. Pass steam from the generator through the mixture.
4. Note the temperature of the distilling vapour (it stays constant below 100 °C).
5. Collect the distillate in a graduated cylinder or separating funnel. Note the volumes of the oil layer and water layer collected over a set time.
6. Convert volumes to masses using densities.
7. Note the atmospheric pressure.

## Observations and calculations

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Boiling temperature of the mixture | ___ °C |
| Atmospheric pressure (P) | ___ mm Hg |
| Vapour pressure of water at that temperature (pw, from tables) | ___ mm Hg |
| Vapour pressure of oil, po = P − pw | ___ mm Hg |
| Volume / mass of oil collected | ___ |
| Volume / mass of water collected | ___ |

1. Theoretical ratio = (po × Mo) / (pw × 18).
2. Actual ratio = mass of oil ÷ mass of water collected.
3. Efficiency = actual ratio ÷ theoretical ratio × 100.

**Worked example (illustration only):** boiling at 95.5 °C, P = 760, pw = 646, po = 114 mm Hg; turpentine (taking M ≈ 136). Theoretical ratio = (114 × 136)/(646 × 18) ≈ 1.33 g oil per g water. If 10 g oil and 9.0 g water were collected, actual ratio = 1.11, efficiency ≈ 83%.

## Result

The mixture distilled at ___ °C. The efficiency of steam distillation was found to be ___%.

## Precautions

1. Keep the steam generator safety tube in place to avoid pressure build-up.
2. Warm the flask slightly so steam does not flood it.
3. Keep the condenser water flowing so the oil does not escape as vapour.
4. Separate layers carefully and allow time for them to settle.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does the mixture boil below 100 °C?** The total vapour pressure is the sum of both liquids' vapour pressures and reaches atmospheric pressure at a lower temperature.
2. **Why is the efficiency less than 100%?** Steam passes through the liquid too quickly to become fully saturated with oil vapour; some heat and vapour are lost.
3. **Give pharmaceutical uses.** Extraction of volatile oils (clove, eucalyptus, peppermint) and preparation of aromatic waters.
4. **What is a Florentine receiver?** A vessel that separates an oil from water by density, with outlets for each layer.
5. **Can steam distillation be used for water-miscible liquids?** No, the method depends on the liquids being immiscible.

# Overall heat transfer coefficient of a heat exchanger

**Aim:** To determine the overall heat transfer coefficient (U) of a given heat exchanger (double-pipe or shell-and-tube), in parallel and counter-current flow.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Hot water lines and steam are hot; do not touch uninsulated pipes.

## Principle

In a heat exchanger, heat passes from the hot fluid to the cold fluid through a metal wall. The rate of heat transfer is:

Q = U × A × ΔTlm

where U is the overall heat transfer coefficient (W/m²·K), A the heat transfer area and ΔTlm the **log mean temperature difference**:

ΔTlm = (ΔT1 − ΔT2) / ln (ΔT1/ΔT2)

ΔT1 and ΔT2 are the temperature differences between the two fluids at the two ends.

The heat given up by the hot fluid (or taken up by the cold fluid) is Q = m × c × (temperature change), where m is the mass flow rate and c the specific heat (4.18 kJ/kg·K for water).

## Requirements

Double-pipe (or shell-and-tube) heat exchanger set-up with hot water tank and heater, cold water supply, valves to switch between parallel and counter flow, four thermometers (or sensors) at the inlets and outlets, rotameters or measuring jar and stopwatch for flow rates.

## Procedure

1. Measure (or note from the set-up) the tube diameter and length; calculate the heat transfer area A = π D L.
2. Heat water in the tank to about 60–70 °C.
3. Set the valves for **parallel flow**. Start hot water through the inner tube and cold water through the annulus at steady, known flow rates.
4. Wait until temperatures are steady (about 10 minutes). Record hot inlet (Th1), hot outlet (Th2), cold inlet (Tc1) and cold outlet (Tc2).
5. Measure both flow rates by collecting water for a known time.
6. Switch to **counter-current flow** and repeat.

## Observations and calculations

| Flow | Hot flow (kg/s) | Cold flow (kg/s) | Th1 | Th2 | Tc1 | Tc2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Parallel | | | | | | |
| Counter | | | | | | |

1. Heat lost by hot water: Qh = mh × 4180 × (Th1 − Th2) W. Heat gained by cold water: Qc = mc × 4180 × (Tc2 − Tc1) W. Use the average Q.
2. Parallel flow: ΔT1 = Th1 − Tc1, ΔT2 = Th2 − Tc2. Counter flow: ΔT1 = Th1 − Tc2, ΔT2 = Th2 − Tc1.
3. ΔTlm = (ΔT1 − ΔT2) / ln (ΔT1/ΔT2).
4. U = Q ÷ (A × ΔTlm).

**Worked example (illustration only):** counter flow, mh = 0.05 kg/s, Th1 = 65, Th2 = 50 °C → Q = 0.05 × 4180 × 15 = 3135 W. Tc1 = 30, Tc2 = 42 °C. ΔT1 = 65 − 42 = 23, ΔT2 = 50 − 30 = 20, ΔTlm = 3/ln(1.15) ≈ 21.5 K. With A = 0.25 m², U = 3135/(0.25 × 21.5) ≈ 583 W/m²·K.

## Result

The overall heat transfer coefficient was ___ W/m²·K in parallel flow and ___ W/m²·K in counter-current flow. Counter-current flow gave better heat transfer.

## Precautions

1. Take readings only after steady state is reached.
2. Keep flow rates constant during a run.
3. Make sure no air is trapped in the tubes.
4. Check that heat lost and heat gained agree reasonably; a large gap means heat loss to surroundings.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the overall heat transfer coefficient?** The rate of heat transfer per unit area per degree of temperature difference across all resistances (films and wall): 1/U = 1/h1 + x/k + 1/h2.
2. **Why use LMTD and not the simple average?** Temperature difference changes along the exchanger in a logarithmic way.
3. **Why is counter-current flow better?** It keeps a larger average temperature difference and lets the cold fluid leave hotter than the hot fluid's outlet.
4. **What is fouling?** Scale or deposit on the surfaces that adds resistance and lowers U.
5. **Differentiate heat exchanger and heat interchanger.** Exchanger uses steam/hot gas as heating medium; interchanger transfers heat between two process fluids.

# Drying curves of calcium carbonate and starch

**Aim:** To construct the drying curve and the rate of drying curve for wet calcium carbonate and wet starch, and to find the critical moisture content.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Use tongs for hot trays.

## Principle

When a wet solid is dried under constant conditions (temperature, humidity and air velocity), its moisture falls in a typical pattern:

- an initial adjustment period,
- a **constant rate period**, when the surface is fully wet,
- the **critical moisture content**, where the rate starts to fall,
- one or two **falling rate periods**, until the solid reaches its **equilibrium moisture content (EMC)**.

Calcium carbonate is a non-porous, non-hygroscopic solid, so most water is unbound and it shows a long constant rate period. Starch holds water inside its granules (bound water), so it shows a shorter constant rate period and a long falling rate period.

## Requirements

Calcium carbonate and starch powders, water, two shallow flat trays (or Petri dishes) of known area, hot air oven (about 60–70 °C) or tray dryer, balance, stopwatch, desiccator, spatula.

## Procedure

1. Weigh each empty, dry tray (W0) and measure its area (A).
2. Mix about 50 g calcium carbonate with enough water (e.g. 25 ml) to form a uniform paste; spread evenly in a tray. Do the same with starch in the second tray.
3. Weigh each tray with wet material (initial weight).
4. Place both in the oven at a fixed temperature (e.g. 60 °C).
5. Remove and weigh quickly every 10 minutes (every 15–20 minutes later on) until two successive weights are nearly constant.
6. Finally dry a small portion to constant weight at 105 °C (or use the final constant weight) to obtain the dry solid weight (Ws).

## Observations and calculations

| Time (min) | Weight of tray + material (g) | Weight of water present (g) | Moisture content X (g water/g dry solid) | Rate of drying (g/m²·min) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | | | | — |
| 10 | | | | |
| 20 | | | | |
| … | | | | |

1. Water present = (tray + material) − W0 − Ws.
2. Moisture content X = water present ÷ Ws.
3. Rate of drying R = (Ws/A) × (ΔX/Δt), or simply loss in weight ÷ (A × time interval).
4. Plot **drying curve:** X against time.
5. Plot **rate of drying curve:** R against average X for each interval.
6. Read the critical moisture content where the constant rate line ends, and the EMC where the rate becomes zero.

**Worked example (illustration only):** tray area 0.02 m²; weight lost in 10 minutes in the constant rate period = 2.0 g. Rate = 2.0 ÷ (0.02 × 10) = 10 g/m²·min.

## Result

1. Drying curves and rate of drying curves were drawn for both materials.
2. Critical moisture content: calcium carbonate ___ ; starch ___ g water/g dry solid.
3. Calcium carbonate showed a longer constant rate period; starch showed a longer falling rate period because of bound water.

## Precautions

1. Spread the material in a uniform thin layer.
2. Keep oven temperature constant; open the door briefly.
3. Weigh quickly so the material does not gain moisture from room air.
4. Use the same balance throughout.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the constant rate period?** The stage in which the surface stays fully wet and evaporation proceeds like that of free water, at a steady rate.
2. **Define critical moisture content.** The moisture content at which the constant rate ends and the rate starts falling.
3. **Why does starch show a long falling rate period?** It holds bound water inside its granules that must diffuse out slowly.
4. **What controls the rate in the second falling rate period?** Diffusion of moisture from the inside of the solid to the surface.
5. **What use is the rate curve?** To estimate drying time, choose a dryer and conditions, and scale up.
practicals.title: Drying curves of calcium carbonate and starch

# Moisture content and loss on drying

**Aim:** To determine the moisture content and the loss on drying (LOD) of a given sample (for example wet granules, starch or a crude drug powder).

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Use tongs and a desiccator for hot bottles.

## Principle

When a moist sample is heated to constant weight, the loss in weight is taken as the water (and any volatile matter) it contained. The result is expressed in two ways:

- **Loss on drying (LOD), wet basis:** LOD (%) = (weight of water ÷ weight of wet sample) × 100
- **Moisture content (MC), dry basis:** MC (%) = (weight of water ÷ weight of dry sample) × 100

LOD can never exceed 100%; MC can exceed 100% for very wet materials. Pharmacopoeias usually specify LOD (for example, drying at 105 °C to constant weight).

Relation: MC = LOD ÷ (100 − LOD) × 100.

## Requirements

Sample, flat glass weighing bottles with stoppers (or Petri dishes), hot air oven at 105 °C (or the temperature given in the monograph), desiccator with silica gel, analytical balance, spatula. A moisture balance (infrared/halogen) can be used for a quick check.

## Procedure

1. Dry an empty weighing bottle with its stopper at 105 °C for 30 minutes, cool in a desiccator and weigh (W1).
2. Put about 1–2 g of the sample in the bottle, spread evenly, and weigh (W2).
3. Place the bottle in the oven with the stopper removed (kept beside it). Dry at 105 °C for the specified time (e.g. 1–2 hours).
4. Close the bottle, cool in the desiccator and weigh.
5. Repeat drying for 30-minute periods until two successive weighings do not differ by more than 0.5 mg (constant weight, W3).
6. Do the test in duplicate.

## Observations and calculations

| Reading | Weight (g) |
| --- | --- |
| Empty bottle (W1) | |
| Bottle + wet sample (W2) | |
| Bottle + dried sample (W3) | |

- Weight of wet sample = W2 − W1
- Weight of water = W2 − W3
- Weight of dry sample = W3 − W1
- LOD (%) = (W2 − W3) ÷ (W2 − W1) × 100
- MC (%) = (W2 − W3) ÷ (W3 − W1) × 100

**Worked example (illustration only):** wet sample 2.000 g, dry sample 1.900 g, water 0.100 g. LOD = 0.100/2.000 × 100 = 5.0%. MC = 0.100/1.900 × 100 ≈ 5.26%.

## Result

Loss on drying of the sample = ___% (wet basis). Moisture content = ___% (dry basis).

## Precautions

1. Bottles must be dried and cooled before the first weighing.
2. Cool in a desiccator before every weighing; never weigh hot.
3. Keep the sample layer thin (not more than about 5 mm).
4. Weigh quickly to prevent moisture pick-up.
5. Do not exceed the specified temperature, or the sample may decompose and give a falsely high result.

## Viva questions

1. **Differentiate LOD and moisture content.** LOD is water per unit wet weight; MC is water per unit dry weight.
2. **Why dry to constant weight?** To make sure all removable moisture has gone.
3. **Why is LOD important for granules?** Too much moisture makes tablets stick and degrade; too little causes capping and poor binding.
4. **What other method measures water specifically?** Karl Fischer titration, which measures water only and not other volatile matter.
5. **What is the purpose of the desiccator?** To let the sample cool without absorbing moisture from air.
practicals.title: Moisture content and loss on drying

# Humidity of air: wet and dry bulb, and dew point

**Aim:** To determine the humidity of air (i) from wet and dry bulb temperatures and (ii) by the dew point method.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Ether (if used in the dew point hygrometer) is highly flammable; keep flames away.

## Principle

**Humidity** is the amount of water vapour in air.

- **Absolute humidity:** mass of water vapour per unit mass of dry air (kg/kg).
- **Relative humidity (RH):** ratio of the partial pressure of water vapour in the air to the saturated vapour pressure at the same temperature, × 100.
- **Dew point:** temperature at which air becomes saturated when cooled at constant pressure, so moisture starts to condense.

**Wet and dry bulb method:** a dry thermometer reads the air temperature (dry bulb). A thermometer whose bulb is covered with wet muslin reads lower (wet bulb), because evaporation of water cools it. The drier the air, the faster the evaporation and the larger the difference (wet bulb depression). From the two readings, RH is read from a **psychrometric chart** or humidity tables.

**Dew point method:** a polished surface is cooled slowly (by evaporating ether or adding ice to water) until dew just appears. The temperature then is the dew point. RH = (saturated vapour pressure at the dew point ÷ saturated vapour pressure at air temperature) × 100.

## Requirements

Wet and dry bulb hygrometer (or sling psychrometer), muslin wick, distilled water, psychrometric chart or humidity tables, dew point hygrometer (Regnault's or a polished metal can), ether or ice, thermometers, aspirator or bellows, table of saturated vapour pressure of water.

## Procedure

**(i) Wet and dry bulb**

1. Wet the muslin around the wet bulb with distilled water.
2. Ventilate the bulbs (whirl the sling psychrometer or use a fan) for 1–2 minutes until the wet bulb reading is steady.
3. Note the dry bulb (Td) and wet bulb (Tw) temperatures. Repeat three times.
4. Read RH and absolute humidity from the chart or tables.

**(ii) Dew point**

1. Place ether (or water) in the polished container with a thermometer.
2. Cool slowly by bubbling air through the ether (or by adding ice bit by bit), stirring.
3. Note the temperature (T1) at which a film of dew first appears on the polished surface.
4. Stop cooling and note the temperature (T2) at which the dew disappears.
5. Dew point = (T1 + T2)/2. Note the room (dry bulb) temperature.

## Observations and calculations

| Method | Reading 1 | Reading 2 | Reading 3 | Mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dry bulb (°C) | | | | |
| Wet bulb (°C) | | | | |
| Dew point (°C) | | | | |

RH (dew point method) = p(dew point) ÷ p(room temperature) × 100.

**Worked example (illustration only):** room temperature 30 °C (saturated vapour pressure about 31.8 mm Hg); dew point 20 °C (about 17.5 mm Hg). RH = 17.5/31.8 × 100 ≈ 55%.

## Result

1. RH by wet and dry bulb method = ___%.
2. Dew point = ___ °C; RH by dew point method = ___%.

## Precautions

1. Use distilled water and a clean wick; ventilate well before reading.
2. Do not touch or breathe on the bulbs or the polished surface.
3. Cool slowly near the dew point so it is not overshot.
4. Keep ether away from flames.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does the wet bulb read lower?** Evaporation of water from the wick takes latent heat from the bulb.
2. **When are wet and dry bulb readings equal?** When the air is saturated (RH 100%), so no evaporation takes place.
3. **Why is humidity control important in pharmacy?** Hygroscopic and effervescent products, gelatin capsules and tablet compression need controlled RH.
4. **What is a psychrometric chart?** A chart relating dry bulb, wet bulb, dew point, humidity and enthalpy of air–water mixtures.
5. **How is air dehumidified?** By cooling below the dew point (refrigeration) or by adsorbents such as silica gel (desiccant wheel).
practicals.title: Humidity of air: wet and dry bulb, and dew point

# Rotary tablet machine, fluidised bed coater, fluid energy mill and dehumidifier

**Aim:** To study and describe the construction, working and applications of pharmaceutical machinery: rotary tablet machine, fluidised bed coater, fluid energy mill and dehumidifier.

> This is a study and description experiment. Do not operate machines without your teacher. Keep hands, hair and loose clothing away from moving parts.

## Principle

Each machine carries out one unit operation used in production: compression (tablet machine), coating (fluidised bed coater), size reduction (fluid energy mill) and air conditioning (dehumidifier). The record should give principle, construction (sketch), working and uses of each.

## Requirements

The machines (or models and charts), record book, pencil and scale.

## Procedure

1. Observe each machine with the teacher; identify every part.
2. Draw a labelled sketch.
3. Note the working steps and the products it is used for.

## Observations

### 1. Rotary tablet machine

**Principle:** powder or granules are compressed between an upper and a lower punch in a die. Many punch–die sets on a rotating turret compress tablets continuously.

**Construction:**

- **Hopper** and **feed frame** (gravity or forced/paddle feeder).
- **Turret (die table)** carrying many dies, with upper and lower punches in tracks.
- **Cams** that raise and lower the punches.
- **Weight-control (fill) cam** and **ejection cam**.
- **Pre-compression and main compression rollers**.
- Take-off blade (scraper) and discharge chute.

```text
     upper punches ↓  ↓  ↓  (moved by upper cam track)
   ════╤══╤══╤══╤══╤══════  turret (die table) rotates
       die die die die
     lower punches ↑  ↑  ↑
   fill → weight adjust → pre-compression → compression → ejection → take-off
```

**Working:** (1) **filling**: lower punch drops and granules fill the die from the feed frame; (2) **weight adjustment**: lower punch rises slightly to push out excess, scraped off; (3) **compression**: punches pass between pressure rollers; (4) **ejection**: lower punch rises and pushes the tablet out; (5) take-off blade guides it to the chute.

**Uses:** large-scale production of tablets, from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand per hour depending on stations and speed. Double-sided machines give two tablets per station per turn.

### 2. Fluidised bed coater

**Principle:** particles or tablets are suspended in an upward stream of hot air while a coating solution is sprayed onto them; the solvent evaporates quickly, leaving a film.

**Construction:** product container with perforated base; air handling unit (fan, filter, heater); **spray nozzle** (top spray, bottom spray with a **Wurster column**, or tangential spray); peristaltic pump for coating liquid; expansion chamber and bag filters.

**Working:** particles are fluidised; coating liquid is atomised onto them; in the Wurster (bottom-spray) type, particles rise through a central partition, are coated, dry in the upper zone and fall back to be coated again, giving a uniform film.

**Uses:** coating of granules, pellets and powders (taste masking, enteric and sustained-release coats); granulation and drying in the same unit.

### 3. Fluid energy mill (jet mill)

**Principle:** attrition and impact between particles moving at very high speed in jets of compressed air or inert gas.

**Construction:** oval loop of pipe with gas nozzles at the bottom, venturi feed inlet, classifier at the outlet leading to a cyclone and bag filter.

**Working:** particles race round the loop, collide and break; fine particles leave through the classifier; coarse ones stay for further grinding. Expanding gas cools the material.

**Uses:** micronising to 1–20 µm: antibiotics, steroids, inhalation drugs, vitamins; thermolabile drugs.

### 4. Dehumidifier

**Principle:** water vapour is removed from air either by **cooling it below its dew point** (refrigerant type) or by **adsorption on a desiccant** (desiccant type).

**Construction:**

- *Refrigerant type:* fan, cooling coil (evaporator), condensate tray and drain, reheating coil, compressor.
- *Desiccant type:* slowly rotating wheel coated with silica gel or lithium chloride; process air passes through one part of the wheel and is dried; a hot reactivation air stream dries the other part.

**Working:** moist room air is drawn in; moisture condenses on the cold coil (or is adsorbed on the desiccant); dry air is returned to the room; RH is set by a humidistat.

**Uses:** maintaining low RH in areas for effervescent granules, hygroscopic powders, gelatin capsule filling, tablet compression and storage; preventing sticking and degradation.

## Result

The construction, working and applications of the rotary tablet machine, fluidised bed coater, fluid energy mill and dehumidifier were studied and recorded with labelled sketches.

## Precautions

1. Machines must be switched off and isolated before parts are examined.
2. Do not insert fingers into dies, turrets or fans.
3. Use guards and follow the standard operating procedure.

## Viva questions

1. **What are the stages of tablet compression in a rotary press?** Filling, weight adjustment, pre-compression and compression, ejection.
2. **What is pre-compression for?** It removes air and gives a first light compression, reducing capping.
3. **What is a Wurster column?** A partition in a bottom-spray fluid bed coater that guides particles past the spray in a regular cycle for uniform coating.
4. **Why is a fluid energy mill suitable for heat-sensitive drugs?** Expansion of compressed gas cools the material, so no heat build-up.
5. **How does a desiccant dehumidifier differ from a refrigerant one?** It adsorbs moisture on silica gel or lithium chloride, and works well at low temperatures and very low RH.
practicals.title: Rotary tablet machine, fluidised bed coater, fluid energy mill and dehumidifier

# Size analysis of tablet granules by sieving

**Aim:** To determine the particle size distribution of given tablet granules by sieve analysis, and to construct size–frequency curves, including cumulative and logarithmic-probability plots.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ.

## Principle

A weighed sample is shaken through a nest of standard sieves arranged with the largest opening at the top. Each sieve retains particles larger than its opening. The weight retained on each sieve gives the distribution of particle sizes. The size of the particles retained between two sieves is taken as the arithmetic mean of the two openings.

From the data:

- **Frequency (histogram) curve:** % retained against mean size.
- **Cumulative curves:** cumulative % undersize (or oversize) against size.
- **Log-probability plot:** cumulative % undersize on a probability scale against log size; a straight line means a **log-normal distribution**. The size at 50% is the **geometric mean diameter (dg)**, and the geometric standard deviation σg = d84.13 / d50.

Average size by weight: d(avg) = Σ (% retained × mean size) ÷ 100.

## Requirements

Granules (about 100 g), set of standard sieves (for example sieve numbers 10, 22, 44, 60, 85 and a receiver pan), lid, mechanical sieve shaker, balance, brush, arithmetic and log-probability graph paper.

## Procedure

1. Clean and weigh each sieve and the pan.
2. Arrange the sieves with the coarsest at the top and the pan at the bottom.
3. Weigh 100 g of granules and place on the top sieve; cover with the lid.
4. Shake on the sieve shaker for 10–20 minutes at a fixed amplitude.
5. Weigh each sieve with its retained granules; find the weight retained.
6. Check that the total equals the sample weight (loss not more than about 1–2%).

## Observations and calculations

| Sieve passed | Sieve retained on | Mean aperture (µm) | Weight retained (g) | % retained | Cumulative % undersize | % × mean size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| — | 10 (1700 µm) | (above 1700) | | | | |
| 10 | 22 (710 µm) | 1205 | | | | |
| 22 | 44 (355 µm) | 532.5 | | | | |
| 44 | 60 (250 µm) | 302.5 | | | | |
| 60 | 85 (180 µm) | 215 | | | | |
| 85 | Pan | (below 180) | | | | |

1. % retained = weight retained ÷ total × 100.
2. Cumulative % undersize = 100 − cumulative % retained on that sieve and above.
3. Average diameter = Σ(% retained × mean size) ÷ 100.
4. Plot the histogram, cumulative undersize and oversize curves, and the log-probability graph. Read d50 and d84.13.

**Worked example (illustration only):** if 40% is retained between sieves 22 and 44 (mean 532.5 µm), 35% between 44 and 60 (302.5 µm) and 25% between 60 and 85 (215 µm), average size = (40 × 532.5 + 35 × 302.5 + 25 × 215)/100 = (21300 + 10587.5 + 5375)/100 ≈ 373 µm.

## Result

The average particle size of the granules was ___ µm. The geometric mean diameter (from the log-probability plot) was ___ µm and the geometric standard deviation ___. The distribution was (normal / log-normal).

## Precautions

1. Sieves must be clean, dry and undamaged.
2. Do not overload the top sieve.
3. Shake for a fixed time; too long breaks granules and gives more fines.
4. Brush particles from the underside of each sieve into the next before weighing.

## Viva questions

1. **What does the sieve number mean?** Roughly the number of meshes per 25.4 mm; a higher number means a smaller opening.
2. **Why is granule size distribution important?** It affects flow, die filling, weight variation, hardness and dissolution of tablets.
3. **What does a straight line on log-probability paper indicate?** The sizes follow a log-normal distribution.
4. **Define geometric mean diameter.** The size at 50% on the cumulative log-probability plot.
5. **What is a limitation of sieve analysis?** It is unreliable below about 40 µm and depends on particle shape; long shaking causes attrition.
practicals.title: Size analysis of tablet granules by sieving

# Laws of size reduction and critical speed of a ball mill

**Aim:** To verify the laws of size reduction using a ball mill, to determine Kick's, Rittinger's and Bond's coefficients and the power requirement, and to calculate the critical speed of the ball mill.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Keep the mill guard closed while it runs.

## Principle

The energy used in size reduction depends on the feed size (L1) and product size (L2):

- **Rittinger's law:** E = KR (1/L2 − 1/L1)
- **Kick's law:** E = KK ln (L1/L2)
- **Bond's law:** E = KB (1/√L2 − 1/√L1)

If the energy used (from power × time) and the average sizes before and after grinding are known, each constant can be calculated. The law that gives the most constant value over several runs fits the material and size range best.

**Critical speed:** the speed at which the balls are carried round with the shell and stop grinding:

Nc = (1/2π) √( g / (R − r) ) revolutions per second

where R is the radius of the mill and r the radius of a ball. Optimum speed is about 0.5–0.75 of Nc.

## Requirements

Laboratory ball mill with motor (power rating known, or a wattmeter), balls, coarse material (e.g. crystals of sodium chloride, calcium carbonate lumps or crushed brick), set of sieves and shaker, balance, stopwatch, tachometer (or count of revolutions), vernier calipers.

## Procedure

1. Measure the inner diameter of the mill (2R) and the diameter of a ball (2r).
2. Find the average size of the feed (L1) by sieve analysis.
3. Load a weighed amount of feed (e.g. 200 g) and balls (about 30–50% of volume).
4. Run the mill for a fixed time (e.g. 10 minutes); note the power (P, watts) and the speed (rpm).
5. Remove the product, separate the balls and find its average size (L2) by sieve analysis.
6. Repeat for different times (e.g. 20 and 30 minutes) with fresh feed.
7. Note the speed at which balls begin to stick to the wall (if the mill has a speed control and window), for comparison.

## Observations and calculations

| Run | Time (s) | Power (W) | Energy E = P × t (J) | L1 (µm) | L2 (µm) | KR | KK | KB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | | | | | | | |
| 2 | | | | | | | | |
| 3 | | | | | | | | |

Energy per unit mass can be used (E ÷ mass of feed). Then:

- KR = E ÷ (1/L2 − 1/L1)
- KK = E ÷ ln (L1/L2)
- KB = E ÷ (1/√L2 − 1/√L1)

**Critical speed:** with R and r in metres, Nc (rpm) = 60 × (1/2π) × √(9.81/(R − r)) ≈ 29.9/√(R − r).

**Worked example (illustration only):** mill diameter 0.30 m (R = 0.15 m), ball diameter 0.02 m (r = 0.01 m). R − r = 0.14 m. Nc = 29.9/√0.14 ≈ 29.9/0.374 ≈ 80 rpm. Optimum about 40–60 rpm.

Energy example: P = 100 W for 600 s → E = 60,000 J for 0.2 kg → 300,000 J/kg. If L1 = 2000 µm and L2 = 500 µm: KK = 300,000/ln 4 ≈ 216,000 J/kg; KR = 300,000/(1/500 − 1/2000) = 300,000/0.0015 = 2.0 × 10⁸ J·µm/kg.

## Result

1. Kick's constant ___, Rittinger's constant ___, Bond's constant ___ (with units).
2. The law giving the most constant value for this material was ___.
3. Critical speed of the ball mill = ___ rpm; optimum operating speed about ___ rpm.

## Precautions

1. Use the same weight of feed and balls in each run.
2. Run at a steady speed below critical.
3. Sieve feed and product in the same way.
4. Power measured includes losses in the motor and mill; note this as a source of error.

## Viva questions

1. **Which law applies to fine grinding?** Rittinger's law.
2. **Which law applies to coarse crushing?** Kick's law.
3. **What happens at critical speed?** Balls are held against the wall by centrifugal force and no grinding occurs.
4. **Why are mixed ball sizes used?** Large balls break coarse feed; small balls fill gaps and do fine grinding.
5. **Why is only a small fraction of energy used for size reduction?** Most is lost as heat, noise, friction and elastic deformation.
practicals.title: Laws of size reduction and critical speed of a ball mill

# Demonstration of colloid mill, planetary mixer, fluidised bed dryer and freeze dryer

**Aim:** To observe the demonstration of major pharmaceutical equipment (colloid mill, planetary mixer, fluidised bed dryer, freeze dryer and similar equipment) and to record their principle, construction, working and uses.

> This is a demonstration. Machines are operated by the teacher or technician only. Stand behind guards and keep clear of moving parts.

## Principle

Each machine performs a unit operation: the colloid mill reduces droplet or particle size by shear, the planetary mixer mixes and kneads, the fluidised bed dryer dries granules by fluidisation, and the freeze dryer dries by sublimation.

## Requirements

The equipment (or models), suitable demonstration material (an oil-in-water emulsion premix, wet granulation mass, wet granules, a frozen solution in vials), record book.

## Procedure

1. Watch the demonstration of each machine and note the steps.
2. Identify and label all parts in a sketch.
3. Record principle, construction, working, uses, merits and demerits.

## Observations

### 1. Colloid mill

**Principle:** **shear**. Material passes through a very narrow gap between a high-speed **rotor** and a stationary **stator**; intense shear breaks droplets or particles to a very small size (often a few micrometres).

**Construction:** a conical rotor turning at high speed inside a matching conical stator; the gap is adjustable (fine clearance, fractions of a millimetre); feed hopper, outlet, cooling jacket.

```text
     feed ↓
   ┌──────────┐
   │ ╲ stator ╱│
   │  ╲rotor ╱ │ ← narrow adjustable gap
   │   ╲    ╱  │
   └────╲__╱───┘ → product
```

**Working:** the premix is fed into the hopper; it is drawn through the gap, sheared and thrown out to the outlet; it may be recirculated.

**Uses:** emulsions, creams, ointments, suspensions, pastes; reducing particle size of insoluble drugs in liquid.

**Merits:** very fine and uniform product; continuous; adjustable gap. **Demerits:** produces heat (cooling needed); not for dry powders; wear of rotor.

### 2. Planetary mixer

**Principle:** the blade turns on its own axis and also travels round the bowl (planetary motion), so the whole bowl is covered.

**Construction:** removable stainless steel bowl; vertical shaft with interchangeable blades (flat beater, whisk, dough hook) driven through planetary gears; speed control; bowl lift.

**Working:** material is placed in the bowl, the blade lowered and the mixer run at the selected speed; granulating fluid is added slowly for wet granulation.

**Uses:** wet granulation, creams, ointments, pastes, small batches.

**Merits:** no dead spots; variable speed; easy cleaning. **Demerits:** batch only; heat on long mixing; limited capacity.

### 3. Fluidised bed dryer

**Principle:** hot air passing up through a bed of wet granules lifts and suspends them, giving fast, uniform heat and mass transfer.

**Construction:** product bowl with perforated base on a trolley; air inlet with filter, fan and heater; expansion chamber with bag filters and shaker; exhaust.

**Working:** wet granules are loaded, the bowl placed in position, hot air started; the bed fluidises; drying is checked by LOD; bags are shaken to return fines; the bowl is removed and emptied.

**Uses:** drying tablet granules; granulation and coating in fluid bed processors.

**Merits:** fast (about 20–40 minutes), uniform, gentle temperature. **Demerits:** attrition and fines; static charge (must be earthed); not for sticky materials.

### 4. Freeze dryer (lyophiliser)

**Principle:** frozen material is dried by sublimation of ice under high vacuum, below the triple point of water.

**Construction:** drying chamber with temperature-controlled shelves; very cold condenser; vacuum pump; refrigeration unit; control panel; stoppering mechanism for vials.

**Working:** freezing on the shelves → vacuum applied → primary drying (gentle shelf heat, ice sublimes and collects on the condenser) → secondary drying (higher shelf temperature removes bound water) → vials stoppered.

**Uses:** antibiotics, vaccines, sera, plasma, enzymes, proteins, injectable powders.

**Merits:** best for very heat-sensitive products; porous, quickly reconstituted cake; long shelf life. **Demerits:** costly; long cycle; hygroscopic product.

## Result

The principle, construction, working and uses of the colloid mill, planetary mixer, fluidised bed dryer and freeze dryer were observed and recorded.

## Precautions

1. Follow the standard operating procedure for each machine.
2. Ensure FBD is earthed and filters are in place before starting.
3. Do not open the freeze dryer chamber under vacuum.
4. Set the colloid mill gap before starting the rotor.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the principle of a colloid mill?** Shear in a narrow gap between a high-speed rotor and a stator.
2. **What is planetary motion in a mixer?** The blade spins about its own axis while revolving around the bowl.
3. **What is fluidisation?** The state in which particles are suspended in an upward gas stream and behave like a boiling liquid.
4. **Name the three stages of freeze drying.** Freezing, primary drying (sublimation), secondary drying (desorption).
5. **Why is the condenser of a freeze dryer kept very cold?** To trap the water vapour as ice so the vacuum is maintained and sublimation continues.

# Factors affecting the rate of filtration and evaporation

**Aim:** To study the effect of (a) surface area, (b) concentration and (c) thickness/viscosity on the rate of filtration and the rate of evaporation.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Handle hot dishes with tongs.

## Principle

**Filtration:** by Darcy's equation, V/t = K A ΔP / (η L). The rate of filtration increases with **filter area (A)** and pressure difference, and decreases with **viscosity (η)** of the liquid and **thickness of the cake (L)**. A more concentrated slurry builds a thicker cake faster, so the rate falls quickly.

**Evaporation:** the rate of evaporation increases with **surface area** exposed and temperature, and decreases as the **concentration** (and so the boiling point and viscosity) of the solution rises.

## Requirements

Funnels of different diameters, filter paper (same grade), measuring cylinders, stopwatch, calcium carbonate (for slurries), glycerin or sucrose (to change viscosity), water; evaporating dishes of different diameters, water bath, balance, sodium chloride or sucrose solutions of different concentrations.

## Procedure

**A. Filtration**

1. *Surface area:* filter equal volumes (e.g. 50 ml) of the same calcium carbonate slurry (e.g. 5% w/v) through funnels of two or three different sizes (filter paper folded in the same way). Note the time to collect a fixed volume of filtrate (e.g. 30 ml).
2. *Concentration:* filter 50 ml of slurries of 2%, 5% and 10% calcium carbonate through the same size funnel. Note times.
3. *Viscosity:* filter 50 ml of water, and of 20% and 40% glycerin (or sucrose) solutions, each containing the same amount of calcium carbonate, through the same funnel. Note times.

**B. Evaporation**

1. *Surface area:* put equal volumes (e.g. 25 ml) of water in dishes of different diameters on the same water bath. Weigh at the start and after 30 minutes.
2. *Concentration:* put 25 ml each of water and of 10%, 20% and 30% sucrose (or sodium chloride) solution in identical dishes on the bath. Weigh at the start and after 30 minutes.

## Observations and calculations

**Filtration**

| Variable | Condition | Time for 30 ml filtrate (s) | Rate (ml/s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Area | Small funnel | | |
| Area | Large funnel | | |
| Concentration | 2% / 5% / 10% | | |
| Viscosity | Water / 20% / 40% glycerin | | |

Rate = volume ÷ time.

**Evaporation**

| Variable | Condition | Initial weight (g) | Weight after 30 min (g) | Loss (g) | Rate (g/min) | Rate per area (g/cm²·min) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Area | Dish 1 (d = __ cm) | | | | | |
| Area | Dish 2 (d = __ cm) | | | | | |
| Concentration | 0% / 10% / 20% / 30% | | | | | |

Rate = loss ÷ time; area of dish = π d²/4.

**Worked example (illustration only):** 30 ml collected in 120 s through the small funnel → 0.25 ml/s; in 60 s through the large funnel → 0.5 ml/s. A dish of 8 cm diameter (area ≈ 50 cm²) lost 6 g in 30 min → 0.2 g/min.

Plot rate against each variable.

## Result

1. The rate of filtration increased with filter area and decreased with increasing slurry concentration and viscosity.
2. The rate of evaporation increased with surface area and decreased with increasing concentration of solute.

## Precautions

1. Use the same grade of filter paper folded in the same way.
2. Stir slurries well before pouring; pour at the same rate.
3. Keep the water bath temperature constant and dishes at the same level.
4. Weigh dishes after wiping the outside dry.

## Viva questions

1. **State Darcy's equation.** V/t = KAΔP/ηL.
2. **Why does a concentrated slurry filter slowly?** It builds a thicker cake quickly, increasing resistance.
3. **How can viscous liquids be filtered faster?** Warm them to lower viscosity, use pressure or vacuum, use a larger area, use filter aids.
4. **Why does a concentrated solution evaporate more slowly?** Its vapour pressure is lower (boiling point higher) and viscosity higher.
5. **Which evaporator increases surface area by forming a thin film?** Film evaporators, such as the climbing film evaporator.
practicals.title: Factors affecting the rate of filtration and evaporation

# Effect of time on the rate of crystallisation

**Aim:** To study the effect of time on the rate of crystallisation of a given substance (for example potassium nitrate, copper sulfate or potash alum) from its supersaturated solution.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Handle hot solutions carefully.

## Principle

**Crystallisation** is the formation of solid crystals from a solution. A hot, nearly saturated solution becomes **supersaturated** on cooling, and the excess solute separates in two steps:

1. **Nucleation:** formation of tiny crystal nuclei.
2. **Crystal growth:** solute deposits on the nuclei.

Supersaturation is the driving force. It is high at first, so crystallisation is fast; as solute separates, the solution approaches saturation and the rate falls. Therefore the amount of crystals formed rises quickly at first and then levels off with time. Slow cooling gives fewer, larger crystals; fast cooling gives many small ones.

## Requirements

Potassium nitrate (or copper sulfate or potash alum), distilled water, beakers, measuring cylinder, water bath or hot plate, thermometer, glass rod, filter paper and funnel (or Buchner funnel), watch glasses, balance, stopwatch, ice bath (optional).

## Procedure

1. Dissolve a weighed amount of solute in water by warming on a water bath (e.g. 40 g potassium nitrate in 50 ml water at about 60 °C), so that the solution will become supersaturated on cooling; filter while hot if needed.
2. Divide equal volumes (e.g. 20 ml) into five identical beakers.
3. Allow all to cool at room temperature without disturbance. Start the stopwatch.
4. At fixed intervals (e.g. 10, 20, 30, 45 and 60 minutes), filter the crystals from one beaker.
5. Dry the crystals between filter papers (or in a warm oven) and weigh.
6. Note the shape and approximate size of the crystals.

## Observations and calculations

| Time (min) | Weight of crystals (g) | Rate over interval (g/min) | % yield |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | | | |
| 20 | | | |
| 30 | | | |
| 45 | | | |
| 60 | | | |

- Rate over an interval = increase in weight ÷ time interval.
- % yield = weight of crystals ÷ theoretical crystal yield × 100, where the theoretical yield = solute present − solute that remains dissolved at the final temperature (from solubility data).

Plot weight of crystals against time, and rate against time.

**Worked example (illustration only):** 3.0 g crystals at 10 min and 5.0 g at 20 min → rate in the second interval = 2.0/10 = 0.2 g/min.

## Result

The weight of crystals increased with time, rapidly at first and then slowly, levelling off as the solution approached saturation. The rate of crystallisation was highest in the first ___ minutes.

## Precautions

1. Use equal volumes of the same solution in identical beakers.
2. Do not disturb or shake the beakers during cooling.
3. Dry all crystal crops in the same way before weighing.
4. Keep the room temperature steady.

## Viva questions

1. **What is supersaturation?** A state in which a solution contains more solute than its equilibrium solubility at that temperature.
2. **Name the two steps of crystallisation.** Nucleation and crystal growth.
3. **Why does the rate fall with time?** The supersaturation (driving force) decreases as solute separates.
4. **How do you get large crystals?** Slow cooling and low supersaturation, so fewer nuclei form and each grows larger.
5. **What is seeding?** Adding small crystals to a supersaturated solution to start crystallisation at a controlled point.
practicals.title: Effect of time on the rate of crystallisation

# Uniformity index of a mix in a double cone blender

**Aim:** To mix a coloured tracer with a powder in a double cone blender and to calculate the uniformity (mixing) index of the mix at different mixing times.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Stop the blender completely before opening it to take samples.

## Principle

A mix is judged by taking several samples from different places and measuring the amount of one component (the **tracer**) in each. In a perfect mix every sample would have the same content. The spread of results is measured by the **standard deviation (s)** of the tracer content of the samples.

- s0 = standard deviation of the completely **unmixed** (segregated) system = √[p(1 − p)], where p is the fraction of tracer.
- sR = standard deviation expected for a **completely random** mix = √[p(1 − p)/n], where n is the number of particles in a sample.
- s = standard deviation actually found.

**Lacey's mixing index:** M = (s0² − s²) ÷ (s0² − sR²). M is 0 for an unmixed system and approaches 1 for a random mix.

A simpler **uniformity index** used in many labs is based on the relative standard deviation (RSD) of the samples: RSD (%) = s ÷ mean × 100. A low RSD means good uniformity.

## Requirements

Laboratory double cone blender, lactose (or starch) as the bulk powder, a coloured or easily assayed tracer (e.g. a water-soluble dye, or sodium chloride/salicylic acid that can be titrated), sample thief or spatula, balance, volumetric flasks, colorimeter (for dye) or titration apparatus, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Weigh the bulk powder (e.g. 490 g lactose) and tracer (e.g. 10 g, so p = 0.02).
2. Load the bulk powder and place the tracer on top in one spot (unmixed start).
3. Run the blender for 2 minutes; stop and take samples (e.g. 1 g each) from at least 6–10 places (top, middle, bottom, both cones).
4. Analyse each sample for tracer (dissolve and read absorbance, or titrate).
5. Replace samples, then repeat sampling after 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes of total mixing.
6. Calculate mean, s, RSD and Lacey's index at each time.

## Observations and calculations

| Mixing time (min) | Tracer content of samples (%) | Mean (%) | s | RSD (%) | M |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | | | | | |
| 5 | | | | | |
| 10 | | | | | |
| 15 | | | | | |
| 20 | | | | | |

s = √[Σ (x − mean)² ÷ (N − 1)], where x is each sample result and N the number of samples.

**Worked example (illustration only):** six samples at 10 minutes read 1.9, 2.1, 2.0, 2.2, 1.8, 2.0% tracer. Mean = 2.0%. Deviations squared: 0.01, 0.01, 0, 0.04, 0.04, 0 = 0.10; s = √(0.10/5) = 0.141; RSD = 0.141/2.0 × 100 ≈ 7.1%.

Plot RSD (or M) against mixing time; find the time after which further mixing gives no improvement (and note any rise due to segregation).

## Result

The uniformity of the mix improved with mixing time; RSD fell from ___% at 2 minutes to ___% at ___ minutes. The mixing index reached ___. The optimum mixing time in the double cone blender was ___ minutes.

## Precautions

1. Stop the blender fully before sampling.
2. Take samples of equal size from fixed, well-spread positions each time.
3. Do not overfill the blender (about 50–60% of volume).
4. Use a tracer of similar particle size and density to the bulk to avoid segregation.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the main mechanism of mixing in a double cone blender?** Diffusive mixing by tumbling.
2. **What does a mixing index of 1 mean?** The mix is as uniform as a random mix can be.
3. **Why can over-mixing reduce uniformity?** Long tumbling can cause segregation of particles differing in size or density.
4. **Why take samples from many positions?** To detect dead spots and segregation anywhere in the blender.
5. **What is geometric dilution?** Mixing a small amount of a potent drug with an equal amount of diluent, then doubling stepwise, to obtain a uniform mix.
practicals.title: Uniformity index of a mix in a double cone blender

1. Reynolds number Re = Duρ/µ (D diameter, u velocity, ρ density, µ viscosity); dimensionless; ratio of inertial to viscous forces.
2. Laminar below about 2000, transition 2000–4000, turbulent above about 4000 (Reynolds' dye experiment).
3. Significance: predicts type of flow; selects friction equation; design of pipes, pumps, mixers; higher Re → faster heat and mass transfer; scale-up.
4. Bernoulli: for steady, frictionless, incompressible flow, total head is constant: P/ρg + u²/2g + Z = constant; real form adds pump work and friction loss.
5. Orifice meter: thin plate with sharp hole in the pipe; manometer across it; fluid accelerates and pressure falls; u0 = C0√(2gΔh), C0 ≈ 0.61; vena contracta. Merits: cheap, simple. Demerits: high permanent pressure loss, less accurate.
6. Venturimeter: converging cone, throat, long diverging cone (about 5–7°); manometer between inlet and throat; Cv ≈ 0.98. Merits: accurate, low pressure loss. Demerits: costly, long, fixed range.
7. Draw both with pressure taps and U-tube.

1. Objectives: correct particle size grade, uniform mixing and dosing, remove oversize and foreign matter, grade granules, particle size analysis, collect dust.
2. Mechanisms: agitation (oscillation, vibration, gyration), brushing, centrifugal, fluid currents.
3. IP grades: coarse (all through sieve 10, NMT 40% through 44); moderately coarse (all 22, NMT 40% through 60); moderately fine (all 44, NMT 40% through 85); fine (all through 85); very fine (all through 120). Sieve number ≈ meshes per 25.4 mm.
4. Cyclone: principle centrifugal force; vertical cylinder + cone, tangential inlet at top, central air outlet, solids outlet at bottom; gas spirals down, particles hit wall and fall, clean gas leaves through centre. Uses: spray dryer and mill product collection. Merits: no moving parts, cheap, continuous. Demerits: poor for very fine particles, needs bag filter after it.
5. Sieve shaker: nest of standard sieves (coarsest on top), lid and pan on a mechanical shaker; weighed sample shaken for fixed time, fraction on each sieve weighed. Uses: size analysis, grading. Merits: simple, reproducible. Demerits: batch, fine cohesive powders clog, attrition.

1. Factors: hardness; toughness (fibrous drugs dried or frozen first); stickiness; softening temperature (cool the mill); moisture (dry < about 5% or wet > about 50%); material structure; physiological effect of potent drugs; purity; feed/product size ratio; bulk density.
2. Hammer mill: principle impact; casing with high-speed rotor carrying swinging hammers, screen at bottom, hopper at top; particles struck repeatedly until they pass the screen. Uses: granules, crude drugs, wet granule sizing. Merits: fast, continuous, size controlled by screen. Demerits: heat, screen clogging, wear, noise.
3. Fluid energy mill: principle attrition and impact in a high-velocity gas stream; oval loop pipe with nozzles at the bottom, venturi feed, classifier at outlet; particles circulate and collide, fines leave. Product 1–20 µm. Uses: micronising antibiotics, steroids, inhalation drugs. Merits: very fine, no heat (gas expansion cools), no moving parts, inert gas possible. Demerits: high gas cost, needs fine feed, dust loss.

questions.answer: Variable-area flow meter. Vertical tapered glass tube, wider at the top, with a float and scale. Fluid flows upward and lifts the float until the annular gap allows the flow; pressure drop across the float stays constant while the area changes. Float height read directly on the scale gives flow rate. Merits: direct reading, cheap, low loss. Demerits: vertical mounting, glass breaks, calibrated for one fluid, not for opaque liquids.
questions.question: Describe the construction and working of a rotameter.

questions.answer: Critical speed is the speed at which balls just start to stick to the wall by centrifugal force: Nc = (1/2π)√(g/(R − r)) rps, about 42.3/√(D − d) rpm (D, d in m). Below it balls slide (attrition only); at about 0.5–0.75 of Nc they cascade (impact + attrition, best grinding); at Nc and above they centrifuge and no grinding occurs. So the mill is run below critical speed.
questions.question: Explain the critical speed of a ball mill and its importance.

questions.answer: Principle: crushing by the weight of heavy rollers plus shearing (attrition). Construction: one or two heavy stone/granite rollers on their edge, moving on a stone bed; roller rotates on its own horizontal axis and around a central vertical shaft; scraper returns material. Working: material crushed and rubbed under the rollers, then sieved. Uses: tough fibrous crude drugs, fine grinding. Merits: little attention, fine powder. Demerits: slow, bulky, not for sticky materials.
questions.question: Write the principle, construction and uses of an edge runner mill.

questions.answer: Measures local (point) velocity. One tube faces the flow (impact opening), another reads static pressure; both joined to a manometer. Fluid striking the impact opening is brought to rest so its kinetic energy appears as pressure: u = C√(2gΔh). Uses: velocity profile in pipes and air ducts, air velocity in dryers. Demerits: point velocity only, many readings needed, solids block it.

questions.answer: Bag filter: chamber with many cloth bags; fan draws dusty air through the cloth; dust is retained and the dust layer itself filters finer particles (to about 1 µm); bags are shaken or reverse-blown to drop dust into a hopper. Used after spray dryers and mills. Air separator: rotating disc spreads feed into an air current driven by a fan; coarse particles fall into an inner cone, fine ones carried to an outer cone; continuous classification, often after a ball or hammer mill.
questions.question: Explain the working of a bag filter and an air separator.

questions.answer: Principle: Stokes' law, v = d²(ρs − ρf)g/18η. In an upward fluid stream, particles settling faster than the fluid velocity settle; smaller ones are carried over. Series of tanks of increasing diameter (decreasing velocity): coarse particles settle in the first, finer ones in later tanks. Uses: grading fine insoluble powders (kaolin, calamine). Merits: gentle, separates fines. Demerits: wet product must be dried, slow, much fluid.
questions.question: Explain the principle and working of an elutriation tank.

questions.answer: Principle: crushing and shearing. Construction: rotating steel mortar with a heavy steel pestle mounted off-centre; pestle turns by friction; scraper keeps material under it; pestle can be lifted for emptying. Working: as the mortar turns the pestle rolls and grinds by compression and shear. Uses: fine grinding of drugs and chemicals. Demerits: batch, slow, not for sticky material.
questions.question: Describe the end runner mill.

questions.answer: Major (frictional) losses in straight pipes: Fanning equation hf = 4fLu²/2gD, or ΔP = 2fρu²L/D; laminar f = 16/Re (Hagen–Poiseuille); turbulent f depends on Re and roughness. Minor losses: sudden expansion, sudden contraction, fittings and valves (expressed as equivalent length), obstructions such as meters. Losses increase with velocity, length and roughness and decrease with pipe diameter.

1. Principle: vapour from one effect heats the next effect, kept at lower pressure, so latent heat is reused.
2. Construction: two or more evaporators in series; steam to the first effect only; condenser and vacuum pump on the last; draw block diagram.
3. Working: steam heats effect 1 → its vapour heats effect 2 (lower pressure, lower boiling point) → its vapour heats effect 3 → last vapour to condenser; liquid becomes more concentrated along the line.
4. Feeding: forward (with steam, no pumps, thickest liquid in coldest effect); backward (pumps needed, thickest liquid in hottest effect, good for viscous); mixed; parallel (crystallising liquids).
5. Economy = kg water evaporated ÷ kg steam used. Single effect slightly below 1; n effects about n times (triple about 2.5). Capacity is not increased because ΔT is shared.
6. Uses: large-scale concentration (extracts, sugar, salt).
7. Merits: large steam saving, lower temperature in later effects. Demerits: high initial cost, complex control, space.
questions.question: Explain the principle, construction and working of a multiple effect evaporator. Discuss its economy and methods of feeding.

questions.answer:
1. Heat transfer: movement of heat from a hotter to a colder body; used in solution making, evaporation, distillation, drying, sterilisation, crystallisation.
2. Conduction: molecule-to-molecule, no bulk movement; Fourier's law dQ/dt = −kA dT/dx; flat wall Q/t = kA(T1 − T2)/x; resistance x/kA; composite walls add in series.
3. Convection: bulk fluid motion, natural or forced; Q/t = hAΔT; film resistance; fouling.
4. Radiation: electromagnetic waves, no medium; Q/t = εσAT⁴; black body, emissivity, Kirchhoff's law.
5. Overall coefficient: 1/U = 1/h1 + x/k + 1/h2; Q/t = UA(LMTD).
6. Heat exchanger: heat from steam/hot gas to process fluid through a wall; heat interchanger: from one process liquid (or gas) to another, for heat recovery.
7. Types: double-pipe; shell-and-tube (1-1, 1-2 pass, baffles); plate exchanger. Counter-current flow gives better transfer than parallel. Draw shell-and-tube.

questions.answer:
1. Steam distillation: immiscible liquids each exert their own vapour pressure; mixture boils when pA + pB = atmospheric, so below 100 °C. Steam from generator passed through drug + water; vapour condensed; oil separated in a Florentine receiver. mA/mB = pA MA/pB MB. Uses: volatile oils (clove, eucalyptus, peppermint), aromatic waters.
2. Reduced pressure: lowering pressure lowers boiling point; Claisen flask, capillary air leak to prevent bumping, condenser, receiver, manometer, vacuum pump, water/oil bath. Uses: thermolabile extracts, high-boiling liquids, solvent recovery.
3. Molecular distillation: very high vacuum (about 10⁻³ mm Hg); distance between evaporating and condensing surfaces less than the mean free path, so molecules travel without collision; thin film. Falling film and centrifugal stills. Uses: vitamins A and E from fish liver oils, refining oils.
4. Diagrams of each set-up earn marks.

questions.answer:
1. Factors: temperature; temperature and time of exposure; pressure (vacuum lowers bp); surface area; type of product (foaming, scaling, viscosity rise); concentration; vapour removal and agitation; economic factors.
2. Climbing film: long vertical tubes in a steam calandria; feed at bottom boils; vapour rises fast and carries a thin film up the walls; separator at top. Uses: thermolabile and foaming liquids. Merits: short contact, high heat transfer, continuous. Demerits: needs large ΔT, high headroom, not for viscous/scaling.
3. Forced circulation: pump drives liquid through tubes at high velocity; liquid kept under pressure, flashes in vapour head; concentrate withdrawn. Uses: viscous, scaling, crystallising liquids. Merits: high transfer coefficient, less scaling. Demerits: pump cost, power, hold-up.

questions.answer: Hemispherical pan (stainless steel/copper) with outer steam jacket; steam inlet, condensate outlet with trap, air vent; may tilt and have a stirrer. Steam condenses in the jacket and boils the liquid at atmospheric pressure. Uses: concentrating thermostable aqueous liquids, syrups. Merits: simple, cheap, easy to clean. Demerits: small heating area that falls with level, open (vapour into room), not for thermolabile, deposits burn.

questions.answer: For miscible liquids with close boiling points. Vapour rises through a fractionating column (plate: bubble-cap/sieve; or packed: Raschig rings) against descending liquid; repeated vaporisation–condensation enriches the vapour in the more volatile component. Part of the condensate returned as reflux. Uses: alcohol–water (up to azeotrope), solvent purification, oil fractions. Based on Raoult's and Dalton's laws.
